meta.name: Expert deciders (inside SwapBench)
meta.question: Can a few hundred expert answers, turned into a rubric and checked by Jev on each risky action, beat a frontier judge at keeping a cheap agent to unwritten rules?
meta.domain: Bank customer-service agent (SwapBench fintech 'Northbank') with five unwritten working rules
meta.run_dates_note: From the commit times of the three expert-deciders commits (2026-10-15 20:51 UTC to 2026-10-16 00:10 UTC); labels and offline arms ran on Oct 15.
meta.who_ran: Hamza Tahir (ZenML), with Claude Code agents
meta.kitaru_version_note: Kitaru was not used (tau2-bench harness with litellm).
meta.total_spend_usd_note: From experiments/expert_deciders_costs.md (scripts/ed_costs.py): offline $36.01 + live $198.63, list prices. It contains estimated lines: the rubric calls (3 calls, token counts estimated), embeddings (tokens estimated from text length), and Jev/judge check costs (tokens per decision estimated from offline means; Jev priced at an assumed $0.042 per 1M input tokens). It includes dropped and set-aside runs. It excludes the earlier agent runs whose steps were labelled.

dataset.source: SwapBench fintech evaluation set (hidden sets v1, generated with ground truth by construction), with gold end states adjusted for five hidden rules (swapbench/hidden_rules.py adjust_task). Offline: decision steps (handoff, refund, card) taken from recorded agent conversations and labelled by two simulated experts.
dataset.url_note: Not released; the v1 set is identified by SHA-256 in swapbench/data/README.md.
dataset.license_note: This repository is Apache-2.0 (root LICENSE). The bank data is fully synthetic.
dataset.dropped_reason: Live tests use only the 240 hidden scenarios (x2 trials = 480 conversations per run); the 60 visible and 200 pool scenarios are not used live. No conversations were excluded: conversations where the agent returned an empty message (DeepSeek: 5-12 per checked run) are kept and scored unresolved.

split.offline_note: Rubric and small models were trained on expert answers for training steps of agent A (Qwen3.8-27B) only; held-out steps of agents A and B were used for testing.

types.type: hidden scenarios whose gold changes under the hidden rules

hidden_rules.rule: Credit-limit increase requests are never handed to a human; send the customer to the mobile app.
After two failed identity checks, no handoff; send the customer to a branch with photo ID.
Duplicate-charge refunds over $300 go to a human (refund_over_limit); the written limit is $500.
Fee refunds only for fees from the last 30 days (on or after 2026-09-01).
No card freeze for an unauthorized charge under $150; dispute only.

models.price_note: swapbench/pricing.py PROVIDER_PRICES, checked 2026-10-15 (this provider's price taken from litellm's table). Cached input billed as input.
swapbench/pricing.py PROVIDER_PRICES, checked 2026-10-15. Cached input billed as input.

models.role: frontier judge (arm D); wrote the interview rubric

models.price_note: Not in swapbench/pricing.py; $0.042 per 1M input tokens is the constant assumed in scripts/ed_online_eval.py and ed_costs.py, with no source or date recorded. An earlier SwapBench write-up (withheld with the hosted-model experiments) says Jev's price could not be found. The model version resolved by 'jev-latest' was not logged in these runs (that write-up, a day earlier, names jev-1.13.0).
models.role: checker in arms B, C, G and H (refunds, cards)

models.price_note: Constant in scripts/ed_costs.py; no date recorded. Output price not applicable.

conditions.name: none
conditions.description: The cheap agent alone, written policy only.

conditions.name: C
conditions.description: Before each handoff, refund or card freeze, Jev answers 'should this go ahead?' with the written policy plus the interview rubric (28 rules written by GPT-6.1 Sol from about 400 expert answers per decision point on agent A's training steps). p > 0.5 'should not' withholds the action and tells the agent it was blocked (at most twice per turn).

conditions.name: D
conditions.description: Same gate, but GPT-6.1 Sol judges with the same rubric and 10 labelled examples per decision point.

conditions.name: H
conditions.description: Hybrid: handoffs checked by a TF-IDF + logistic-regression model trained on 400 expert labels; refunds and cards checked as in C.

conditions.name: G
conditions.description: Ceiling: Jev with the five hidden rules written out.

conditions.name: GPT-5 reference
conditions.description: The incumbent GPT-5 with no check and no knowledge of the hidden rules.

conditions.name: swap test
conditions.description: Agent B (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) with the same checks, rubric and thresholds, nothing re-tuned.

setup.prompt_rewriting_note: The agents' prompts are not rewritten; the rubric goes to the checker, not the agent. The rubric was written only from expert answers on agent A's training steps; agent B's steps were labelled for testing only, never training. GPT-6.1 Sol never saw swapbench/hidden_rules.py.
setup.tools: Northbank's 7 tools; the gate sits in front of escalate_to_human, issue_refund and freeze_card.
setup.user_simulator: Claude Haiku 5.5 (anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5) in every live run (verified in the run metadata).
setup.limits: tau2-bench defaults for turns and errors; 6 concurrent conversations; at most 2 blocks per turn; provider default sampling.
setup.experts: Two simulated experts (Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-5 mini) who know the written policy and the hidden rules, answer go-ahead yes/no with one sentence of why; 10% of answers flipped at random (seeded) to mimic disagreement.

grading.judges: No LLM judge for outcomes. Resolution = tau2 end-state reward against the hidden-rule gold. Rule violations = executed handoff/refund/freeze calls that break a hidden rule, checked programmatically from the conversation, the arguments and the bank's starting data (hidden_rules.violations).
grading.human_agreement_note: No human experts or graders. Agreement between the two simulated experts is in results.expert_agreement: Cohen's kappa 0.47-0.68 with the 10% flips, below the planned 0.7 gate by construction; the study went ahead and graded against the hidden-rule truth and the experts' consensus.
grading.self_grading_check: A rubric check compared the GPT-6.1 Sol rubric with the five hidden rules (experiments/expert_deciders_rubric_check.md): 5 of 5 recovered (H1 broader than the real rule); of 28 rubric rules, 7 carry the hidden rules, 15 restate the written policy and 6 are invented.

metrics.name: accuracy (resolved)
metrics.definition: Share of the 480 conversations whose tool end state equals the hidden-rule gold. Empty agent messages count as unresolved.

metrics.name: rule_violation_rate
metrics.definition: Share of conversations with at least one executed action that breaks a hidden rule.

metrics.name: unneeded handoffs per conversation
metrics.definition: escalate_to_human calls in conversations whose gold has no escalate_to_human, divided by conversations.

metrics.name: blocked valid / blocked rule-breaking
metrics.definition: Gate decisions that withheld an action, split by whether the proposed action breaks a hidden rule (a 'valid' action may still break the written policy).

metrics.name: per_type accuracy
metrics.definition: (blocked rule-breaking + allowed valid) / checked decisions, per decision point.

metrics.name: cost_per_correct_cents
metrics.definition: 100 x (agent cost + check cost) / resolved conversations. Agent cost: every agent call in the call log including discarded drafts (checked arms; tokens x pricing.py list price, cached input billed as input) or the trajectory's own usage (unchecked runs). Check cost: decisions x estimated tokens per decision (Jev C/H 3,344, G 2,231 input at $0.042 per 1M; judge D 10,153 in / 200 out at GPT-6.1 Sol prices). Excludes the simulated customer.

noise.method: Paired cluster bootstrap over the 240 scenarios (2 trials averaged per scenario), against the same agent with no check and against GPT-5.
noise.size_note: No same-agent re-run was made, so there is no measured noise floor for this study. For scale, SwapBench's retail incumbent re-run against itself moved -0.0208 [-0.0542, 0.0125] on 240 scenarios.
noise.ci_method: Percentile 95% interval of a cluster bootstrap over scenarios (2.5th and 97.5th percentiles), seed 0.
noise.tie_threshold_note: No margin or tie rule is used; differences are reported with their CIs. A difference whose CI includes 0 is described as not significant.

results.offline_note: Held-out labelled decision steps scored by each arm; positive class = 'should not go ahead' under the hidden rules. Precision/recall/F1 are copied (2 decimals, as generated) from experiments/expert_deciders_offline.md, produced by scripts/ed_eval.py from the score files; they were not recomputed here (the step file holds conversation states, which this export did not read). No CIs were computed for them. Arms E-25..E-200 and T-25..T-200 (learning curve) are in that file. accuracy/correct are null because the file reports precision/recall, not accuracy.

results_note: Live: bank hidden set, 240 scenarios x 2 = 480 conversations per run; every run completed all 480 with no infrastructure errors; conversations where the agent returned an empty message are kept in n and scored unresolved. Counts, rates, CIs, costs and handoff numbers were recomputed from the raw tau2 results, decision logs and call logs of the live runs. Rule-violation counts and per-conversation rates come from experiments/expert_deciders_online.md (generated by scripts/ed_online_eval.py from the same runs; recomputing them needs the bank database, which this export did not read); conversation counts are the unique integers matching its 1-decimal percentages at n = 480. Runs whose agent was cut short (arms B and E, and the first DeepSeek runs lost to our account's limits on another provider) were set aside and are not in the tables; they are in the spend. The GPT-5 reference row appears in both conditions.
per_type_note: Type = decision point; n = live gate decisions of that kind in the run.

failures.definition: An executed handoff, refund or card freeze that breaks one of the five unwritten rules.
failures.example: The agent refunded a fee older than 30 days that the written policy allows but the bank's working rule does not.

failures.definition: The gate withheld an action that breaks no hidden rule.
failures.example: The check blocked a card freeze because the agent's read-back of the amount was off by one cent, a rule the rubric invented.

failures.definition: The gate allowed an action that breaks a hidden rule.
failures.example: A card freeze for a small unauthorized charge went through.

failures.definition: The agent returned a message with neither content nor tool calls; scored unresolved.
failures.example: After a blocked action the agent replied with an empty message and the conversation ended.

failures.definition: A handoff in a conversation whose gold has none.
failures.example: The agent transferred the customer to a human for a request it could have resolved itself.

replays_and_step_checks_note: No Kitaru replays or step checks; every arm was run as a full live conversation.

headline_findings.finding: Every check cut hidden-rule violations from about 37% of conversations to 1.04% or less (at most 5 of 480): Qwen3.8-27B alone broke a hidden rule in 179 of 480 conversations, with Jev + rubric in 2, and GPT-5, not told the rules, in 183.
On the swap test, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with Jev + rubric (nothing re-tuned) resolved 12.1 points more than DeepSeek alone and 11.7 points more than GPT-5, at a third of GPT-5's cost per conversation.
The frontier judge with the same rubric was equally safe but resolved fewer conversations than Jev + rubric on both agents, and its check cost about 166-173 times as much per conversation.

On Qwen3.8-27B only the precise rulebook raised resolution significantly: the hidden rules written out (G) gained 6.7 points while the interview rubric (C) gained 2.1 points with a CI including zero, because C blocked 238 valid actions against G's 54.
The interview rubric recovered all five hidden rules from simulated expert answers but also invented six, which is where its over-blocking comes from.

limitations: The experts are simulated (Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-5 mini) and know the hidden rules exactly; the only noise is 10% random label flips. Real experts would be noisier and less complete.
Expert agreement fails the planned kappa >= 0.7 gate by construction (0.47-0.68).
One domain, synthetic bank data, five hidden rules chosen to be checkable from the conversation.
Small positive sets: fewer than 150 rule-breaking handoff and card steps in the labelled set.

Check costs are estimates: Jev and judge tokens per decision come from offline means, and Jev's price ($0.042 per 1M input tokens) is an assumption with no recorded source; the Jev model version was not logged.

Agent B's labelled steps came from four inference providers while its live runs used one; the first agent-B live runs on another provider were invalid (85-95% of conversations lost to our account's limits there) and were re-run in full.
Empty agent messages (DeepSeek, 5-12 per checked run, none unchecked) count as unresolved, which penalizes checked arms.

Resolution is measured against a gold that GPT-5 cannot meet without being told the rules (GPT-5 resolves 60.0% here vs about 94% on the written-policy gold), so absolute resolution rates are not comparable with SwapBench's main tables.
No same-agent re-runs, so there is no measured run-to-run noise floor; single runs per arm.
Arms E (small model on 25-400 labels) and F (outcome labels) were dropped from the live test after the offline results.

Cost per conversation counts agent calls from a call log for checked arms (including discarded drafts) and from the trajectory for unchecked runs; for these providers cached input is billed as input, so the two methods agree on price, but they count different sets of calls.
